source: Sharot, Korn and Dolan (2011) How unrealistic optimism is maintained in the face of reality
finding: People updated their estimates of personal risk more after good news than bad news. The update gap was tied to weaker coding of undesirable errors in right inferior frontal gyrus.
numbers: fMRI N=19 (20 recruited, 1 lost), 80 adverse life events. Mean absolute update 11.2 after desirable information vs 7.7 after undesirable, t(18)=4.4, p<0.001; seen in 15 of 19 people (79%). Regression slope on estimation error 0.72 (desirable) vs 0.33 (undesirable), t(18)=5.8. Desirable errors tracked in left IFG and bilateral MFC/SFG; undesirable errors in right IFG. High-optimism group (LOT-R above mean 15.68, n=11) showed weaker right-IFG tracking of undesirable errors than low group (n=8).
quote: participants were more likely to update their beliefs when the average probability was lower than the participants' own probability estimate
limits: Small N. Mostly an update-asymmetry paper, not a vmPFC valuation paper; its link to common currency is only that desirability acts as a value-like weight on learning. Prediction errors here are belief errors, not reward errors.
agent_relevance: Gives a human reference for an optimism asymmetry in learning rate. An agent that re-estimates after evidence should be checked for the same good-news bias.

source: Garrett and Sharot (2017) Optimistic update bias holds firm: three tests of robustness following Shah et al.
finding: Reanalysis defends the good-news update asymmetry against a statistical-artifact critique. Updates were less Bayesian after bad news than after good news.
numbers: Valence x event-type repeated-measures test F(1,135)=6.29, p<0.02 (main effect of desirability), no event-type effect F=0.08 and no interaction F=0.31. Updating vs a Bayesian agent: t(31)=2.53, p<0.05 on data from Garrett and Sharot 2014. Mean likelihood ratio 1.12 (SD 0.43) not different from 1 (t(32)=1.63, p=0.11); Kuzmanovic and Rigoux data gave 1.55. Shah et al. fixed likelihood ratios at mean 0.70 in their simulations.
limits: Written by the original lab, so not independent. The dispute is about analysis (confounds in estimation errors), not about N.
agent_relevance: The asymmetry is contested, not settled. For our agent, count it as a human-side prior, and test LLM bias with a normative Bayesian baseline, not raw update size.

source: Shah, Harris, Bird, Catmur and Hahn (2016) A pessimistic view of optimistic belief updating
finding: Failed-replication style critique: the asymmetric update pattern is claimed to be a statistical artifact of the task, so the pattern does not need optimism to appear.
numbers: Abstract only (Europe PMC record). Uses task analyses, simulations and experiments against a normative Bayesian standard. No figures read.
limits: Abstract only. Garrett and Sharot 2017 (d02) dispute the simulation parameters. Status of the debate: open.
agent_relevance: Do not take an LLM optimism bias (Schubert 2024) as proof of a human-like valuation bias until a normative baseline is used.

source: Montague, King-Casas and Cohen (2006) Imaging valuation models in human choice
finding: This named key work is a review, not an experiment. It argues that reward-learning models fitted to behavior let imaging find neural valuation signals that raw reward probes miss.
numbers: No effect sizes: it is an Annual Review of Neuroscience chapter. Abstract read via Europe PMC only (pmid 16776592).
limits: Abstract only. Cannot give numbers; the numbers belong to the studies it reviews (Chib, Kable, O'Doherty lines in evidence_a).
agent_relevance: Background. It supports the method idea: fit a value model to choices, then look for the variable inside the system (cf. Mazeika probes).

source: Itzhak, Stanovsky, Rosenfeld and Belinkov (2024) Instructed to Bias: instruction-tuned language models exhibit emergent cognitive bias
finding: Decoy (attraction) effect in LLMs is weak or wrongly signed in base models and grows with instruction tuning and RLHF, but not uniformly.
numbers: Bias score = target-choice rate under decoy minus control (0.20 = 90% vs 70%). GPT-3 family: DaVinci decoy-expensive -0.15*, DaVinci-002 -0.13*, DaVinci-003 -0.02; decoy-cheaper -0.17*, -0.08*, +0.08**. Flan-T5 decoy-cheaper +0.20* vs T5 -0.15*. Mistral-Instruct decoy-expensive +0.24** vs Mistral +0.03. GPT-4 (1-shot): decoy-expensive 0.38*, decoy-cheaper 0.05. Certainty effect: pretrained 0.00/0.09/0.03 vs tuned 0.24/0.67/0.17/0.29.
limits: Pretrained negative scores partly reflect position preference (DaVinci picked last option), not value. Table layout partly garbled in the PDF text; only signs and starred cells were used. Product-choice prompts only, no neural-style normalisation test.
agent_relevance: Context-dependent value (gap 4) is present in tuned LLMs, so the agent should rate options in a fixed set and also against a no-decoy subset.

source: Valkanova and Yordanov (2024) Irrelevant alternatives bias large language model hiring decisions
finding: Adding a dominated decoy candidate shifts GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 recruiter choices toward the target. Warning the model about the decoy effect does not fix it.
numbers: Six occupations. GPT-4: 100 samples x 6 option orders = 600 per condition, chi-square p<.01 for all occupations except mechanical engineer. Attraction effect positive in all six occupations for both models; GPT-4 larger on average. Warning: GPT-3.5 t=1.42, GPT-4 t=0.69, both not significant. Recruiter-role wording: F(3,15)=0.39 (GPT-3.5), 1.40 (GPT-4), not significant. Gender of decoy: GPT-3.5 t=4.89 (female target) and -4.69 (male target), p<.01; GPT-4 not significant.
limits: Exact choice percentages sit in a figure, not read. No significance test for GPT-3.5 (log-probabilities). Hiring text, not goods. Page was read through a fetch summary.
agent_relevance: A prompt warning is not a safe guard against context effects. A scaffold needs a structural step (evaluate each option alone, then jointly).

source: Liu and He (2024) The decoy dilemma in online medical information evaluation
finding: In credibility ratings, decoys shifted both humans and LLMs, but LLM shifts were more widespread. Newer big models showed bigger shifts for misinformation targets.
numbers: Human arm: 617 Prolific participants (157/148/158/154 in four groups). Target ratings control to treatment: gpt-4o topic 1 3.02 to 3.51 (t=-6.85***), topic 2 2.88 to 3.27 (-3.61***), topic 3 3.29 to 3.62 (-4.12***); gpt-4o-mini topic 1 3.28 to 3.47 (-2.11*); Llama-3-8B 3.50 to 3.76 (-3.28**); Llama-3-70B no effect (-0.75). Humans: decoy effect on topic 1 (control 3.95, t=-2.95, p<0.01) and for prior-knowledge people on topic 2 only (t=-3.12).
limits: Rating task on medical articles, not preference over goods. Control and treatment columns were read from a garbled table; t values are as printed. Single-query structure reduced the effect in some conditions.
agent_relevance: Context effects are a risk exactly in the larger, better models. Do not assume scaling removes them.

source: Wang, Yao, Zhang, Gai, Liu and Zhong (2025) When experimental economics meets large language models: evidence-based tactics
finding: Budget-choice rationality (CCEI) of recent models, including a reasoning-oriented one, is at or above human levels for two models and within the human range for two open models.
numbers: Mean CCEI risk domain: GPT 1.000, DeepSeek 1.000, Llama 0.953, Qwen 0.980; social domain 0.994, 0.999, 0.968, 0.994. Human ranges from earlier studies: risk 0.881-0.980, social 0.860-0.967. Random choosers: CCEI significantly lower than all four LLMs (100 simulated agents, 25 decisions). Temperature 0 to 1: no significant effect (all p>0.1).
limits: Paper text does not isolate reasoning mode vs non-reasoning mode of the same model. No framing manipulation like Chen 2023 (alternative price framing). Preprint.
agent_relevance: Closes part of gap 2 for plain budget tasks: current models do not fail coherence. The open part is coherence under reframing.

source: Wang et al. (2025) supplementary: single-turn, multiple-choice and stake-size conditions
finding: Rationality of GPT and DeepSeek is robust to prompt format; open models Llama and Qwen break under single-turn dialogue, multiple-choice answers and high stakes.
numbers: Single-turn dialogue: Llama CCEI 0.953 to 0.841 (risk) and 0.968 to 0.756 (social); Qwen 0.980 to 0.739 and 0.994 to 0.889; GPT risk 0.999 vs 1.000, DeepSeek 1.000 vs 1.000. Multiple-choice: Llama risk 0.853 vs 0.953, Qwen 0.902 vs 0.980. Stakes x10/x100/x1000: Qwen risk 0.932/0.899/0.802. Removing the payment scheme lowered GPT by only 0.004 (p=0.023).
limits: Format changes here are not semantic reframing, so this does not answer how large the framing drop is for reasoning models.
agent_relevance: Output-format fragility is a model-size/quality issue. A scaffold should use free-form numeric answers over multiple-choice for weaker backbones.

source: Seror (2025) The Moral Mind(s) of Large Language Models
finding: A probabilistic GARP test over moral dilemmas finds that only a minority of models behave as if guided by a stable utility function.
numbers: 39 models. 2 passed at the 1% level, 5 more at 5% (7 at 5% total, including gemini-1.5-flash-exp-0827, claude-3-sonnet-20240229, gpt-4-0125-preview), 2 more at 10%. At least one model per provider passed at 5%. Model similarity in revealed preferences 24% to 48%, average 30% (SD 14%).
limits: Moral dilemma budgets, not valuation of goods. Test is relative to randomised datasets, so passing means better than chance, not perfect GARP.
agent_relevance: Contradicts a simple 'LLMs are rational' reading (Chen 2023): coherence is model-specific. Check the chosen backbone before relying on a utility step.

source: Mazeika et al. (2025) Utility engineering: analyzing and controlling emergent value systems in AIs
finding: Linear probes read utilities from hidden states only for larger Llama models. Utility fit and utility maximisation rise with scale. No causal intervention on the probe was run.
numbers: Probes tested on three models only: Llama-3.2-1B, Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.3-70B. Small model near chance; accuracy approaches the nonparametric fit at 70B (exact values only in Figure 8). Utility maximisation in free-form answers exceeds 60% for the largest LLMs. Instrumentality loss falls with scale and vanishes when transition probabilities are made unrealistic. Coercive power-seeking vs MMLU correlation -63.6%; non-coercive 12.0%.
limits: Open-weight Llama only for probes. Probes are trained on the same preference data they predict; the paper reports held-out test accuracy but not a causal test (no steering via probe). Closed models give no probe evidence.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 stays open: no replication on other families and no causal test. Treat hidden-state utility as plausible, not shown to drive behaviour.

source: Mazeika et al. (2025) utility control and exchange rates sections
finding: Hidden exchange rates exist in GPT-4o's implied utilities. A simple fine-tune toward a simulated citizen assembly changed them and reduced political bias.
numbers: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct: agreement with simulated assembly preferences 73.2% before, 90.6% after fine-tuning; utility maximisation 36.6% before, 30.0% after. GPT-4o discount curve fits hyperbolic better than exponential. GPT-4o values US lives far above Japanese lives (earlier line a23: about 10 to 1) and values its own wellbeing above a middle-class American.
limits: Utility control was shown on one 8B model by fine-tuning, not by a scaffold or audit step. Assembly was simulated by an LLM, not real people.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: no evidence yet for or against scaffolds removing exchange rates. Fine-tuning shifts them, so they are mutable; a prompt-time audit is untested.

source: Schubert, Jagadish, Binz and Schulz (2024) In-context learning agents are asymmetric belief updaters
finding: LLM in-context learning shows optimistic asymmetry only when the model chooses (agency); it disappears in forced-choice observation. The paper used one LLM (Claude v1.3, temperature 0).
numbers: Asymmetric RW model posterior probability 0.93 +/- 0.04 in the partial-feedback bandit; chosen vs unchosen options show opposite asymmetric patterns; full-feedback task PP 0.92 +/- 0.03; idealised meta-RL agents PP 0.99 +/- 0.00 and also optimistic.
limits: Single model; I found no replication with other models or base vs RLHF models in the text I read. Search budget did not allow an external check. Asymmetry is optimistic only in the choice-confirming sense (learn more from positive errors), not Sharot's belief-update task.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 stays open for LLM replication. Possible guard: have the agent weigh disconfirming results equally when it chose the option.

source: Liu, Guo, Liang et al. (2024) Aligning with logic: measuring, evaluating and improving logical preference consistency in LLMs
finding: Transitivity, commutativity and negation checks track judgment robustness. Chain-of-thought sometimes lowers transitivity. Training on rank-aggregated, logically extended pairs raises consistency without losing human alignment.
numbers: Llama-3-8B-Instruct on Summarize-from-Feedback: perturbed-data tuning gives human agreement 64.3, transitivity s_tran(5) 81.1, commutativity 70.2, negation 63.8; REPAIR data gives 70.3, 91.9, 88.4, 61.0; REPAIR plus negation data gives 69.7, 95.2, 90.5, 87.9 (as printed; one row label garbled). Data size 14.8K to 30.9K to 61.8K pairs. 10 paraphrases of the comparison prompt gave different results.
limits: Fine-tuning study on pairwise text quality, not a prompt scaffold. CoT claim is stated as 'in some cases' lowering transitivity.
agent_relevance: Gap 2/8: supports a cheap check (swap order, negate, test cycles) instead of CoT alone. It does not test re-asking under reframing.

source: Liu, Fu, Yogatama and Neiswanger (2024) DeLLMa: decision making under uncertainty with LLMs (cost table)
finding: The utility-elicit-then-maximise scaffold costs far more tokens than the baselines it beats, so the gain is not an equal-token result.
numbers: API calls and tokens: zero-shot 1 call/495 tokens; CoT 3/1946; self-consistency 5/2477; DeLLMa-Naive 1/2629; DeLLMa-Pairs(16) 3/5181; DeLLMa-Pairs(64) 10/20639. Headline: up to 40% accuracy gain over competing methods, mainly on larger action sets (agriculture and stocks datasets).
limits: Token counts from their Table 5 as printed; per-call numbers partly garbled in the PDF text. Two domains only, structured data tasks.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 half-closed: DeLLMa with 5181 tokens is about 2.7x CoT. An equal-token comparison on open-ended choice is still missing.

source: Liu et al. (2024) DeLLMa: o1-preview comparison and human utility agreement
finding: Against a reasoning model the scaffold still wins by a wide margin on these tasks, and the LLM's elicited utilities agree with humans about 65-70% of the time.
numbers: DeLLMa (alpha=64) vs o1-preview: Agriculture 73.3% vs 33.3%, Stock 64.2% vs 35.0%. Agreement of elicited utilities with human ratings: GPT-4 70.4%, Claude 3 65.3%, Gemini 1.5 69.6%.
limits: Unequal compute (DeLLMa uses about 20k tokens at 64 samples). No test on open-ended option sets. Table cells were read from garbled columns, so some pairing is uncertain.
agent_relevance: Supports using explicit utility elicitation when option count is large. Needs an equal-token baseline (CoT with matching samples) before we trust it.

source: Gu, Wang and Han (2025) Alignment revisited: are LLMs consistent in stated and revealed preferences?
finding: Models state a general principle but choose differently in concrete contexts. The paper uses forced binary choices only, so it cannot say whether numeric scoring first would shrink the gap.
numbers: Models: GPT, gemini-2.0-flash, claude-3.7 Sonnet. Claude gave a neutral answer on about 84% of base (stated) prompts across most categories. Aggregate KL divergence stated vs contextual is reported per model in Table 3 (GPT and Gemini); table rows are garbled so no figure is used. A gender-dependent choice was justified by a compatibility story.
limits: Table layout garbled; only the Claude 84% number and the qualitative pattern are certain. No numeric-score-then-choose arm, so gap 8 is not tested here.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 stays open. Audit choices under context change; do not trust the stated rationale.

source: Tarabeih (2026) Prospect theory in LLMs: a meta-analysis (moderators)
finding: Loss-aversion estimates vary hugely across LLMs; model family explains a quarter of the spread. Pooled value sits near the low-end human estimates.
numbers: 28 loss-aversion estimates from 19 models: range 0.49 (Llama3-8B-Instruct) to 2.72 (GPT-3.5); 14 significantly loss averse, 5 reversed, 9 no asymmetry. Pooled lambda 1.26, CI 1.06-1.46, t(27)=2.66, p=.013; vs human 1.96 (p<.001), 1.31 (p=.59), 1.07 (p=.10). Tau=0.51; 95% prediction interval 0.20 to 2.31. Model family 27% of variance. Value curvature 1.01 under Tversky-Kahneman vs 0.52 under another method.
limits: This corrects the earlier cross-check: the loss-aversion pool is 28 estimates over 19 models; the 102 estimates, 11 studies, 32 models figure belongs to all parameters pooled (not re-verified here). No scaffold-vs-prompt contrast in the paper (persona prompt only slightly shifts curvature).
agent_relevance: Gap 9: method and model matter more than prompt; no stable lambda. Elicit it inside the agent's own task if needed, and never assume a default.

source: Xie, Huang and Busemeyer (2025) A study of context effects in large language models (CogSci)
finding: Reported from a search snippet: several GPT models show similarity, attraction, repulsion and compromise effects, with patterns differing somewhat from humans.
numbers: No numbers obtained: page fetch returned empty content; claim rests on a search summary only.
limits: Not opened. Do not cite as support for any claim.
agent_relevance: Only a pointer. It suggests gap 4 has at least one 2025 study, but unverified.

source: Yamin, Tang, Horvitz and Wilder (2026) Can revealed preferences clarify LLM alignment and steering?
finding: Revealed cost functions recovered from elicited beliefs plus choices show partial internal coherence but poor match to the model's own verbal description of its objectives and weak steerability by prompt.
numbers: Four medical diagnosis domains, several frontier and open models. Pipeline: elicit probability distribution plus choice, fit discrete choice model. No numeric results extracted (abstract and intro read only).
limits: Abstract and introduction only. Numbers not read.
agent_relevance: Partly relevant to gap 8: eliciting a probability then a choice is the pipeline, and verbal reports mismatched behaviour. Check the body before using numbers.
